# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

insights.line: What would make it clearly worth it?

whys.g1: Trying a borrowed pair at a matinee and wanting it to catch audience questions in a big hall are two different asks, and the end-seat answer is a workaround, so none of the three clearly belongs with another and leaving each on its own is fair.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer here, and Tomás's end-seat workaround, which doesn't really say what would make it worth it, was left on its own rather than grouped.

founder.order_why: The look-back window (screen 4) sits between two screens that both define where the idea applies (3 and 5), so it breaks up the context step instead of following it.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 5 carry the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies.'), so it reads as the same context screen shown twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asks what it costs or who pays: the glasses at $599 plus an optional $20/month Pro plan, that the wearer pays and it's HSA/FSA eligible, and what they spend today on captioning apps and hearing-aid extras. There is also no screen for the commitment step (order the caption glasses with 15-day free returns), and nothing asks that the glasses need a paired phone with internet.

PRIMARY.order_why: It went from whether I lost a conversation this week to the idea and then to whether I'd use it, which is how I'd think it through, though the table question assumed a setting I never said mine was.
PRIMARY.missing: Nobody asked what I do now when I lose the thread, like lipreading, asking people to repeat, a phone captioning app or just nodding along. Nobody asked where it happened either (restaurant, work, family), what it cost me, or what the glasses would cost and whether they'd work with my hearing aids.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what AirCaps does better, Keel shows back what it will test, which is the obvious next step before I commit to it.
screens.why2: "More of the talk followed" is a clumsy noun phrase I wouldn't say, and dropped into the belief it gives "would have given them more of the talk followed", which takes a second read.
screens.why3: Whether captions let my wearers follow more without asking for repeats is exactly what I hear from users and testimonials every week.
screens.why4: One benefit row, under 9 words, with nothing overlapping and nothing today's way (lipreading, hearing aids, asking people to repeat) already gives, and I can add more if I want.
screens.why5: It still means my "Following more without asking anyone to repeat", and the hard case "the last time they lost the conversation with hearing people" is my problem in my words.
screens.why7: The single row is a noun phrase naming the change against today's way, at most 9 words, and the belief carries it against the problem clause (the time they lost the conversation), not some last conversation that went fine, with the No difference / Worse bar set by Keel.
screens.instead: Keep the row but word it "Following more of the talk without asking for repeats", so the belief reads "...would have let them follow more of the talk without asking for repeats."

screens.why1: Once I've said what it fits into and what it does better, asking what my wearers have to do to start using it is the obvious next question in the solution step, and it is labelled 4 of 4 as the last solution item.
screens.why2: 'What will they have to do to start using it?' with 'setup, extra steps or learning' reads plainly the first time, and I answered it straight off in my own words.
screens.why3: I know exactly what using AirCaps asks of a wearer: putting the glasses on for conversations and keeping them charged.
screens.why4: The only option is the free-text box with its single escape, 'I'm not sure', which fits a founder who can't name the effort, and the hint's limits (up to four, 9 words each) are clear.
screens.why5: My two efforts, 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations; Charge the glasses every day', sit on the screen as I typed them, in the r24 wording of the glasses row.
screens.why7: The box asks for the card's shape (1 to 4 efforts, at most 9 words each, steps the wearer takes themselves, 'I'm not sure' leaving the dimension out), and my rows meet it: base-form verbs in their voice, no sign-off and no overlap with Compatibility's phone and face-watching rows; the only bend is that 'start using it' and the hint lean to one-time setup and don't name a new habit, though my habit rows came through anyway.
screens.instead: What will they have to do to start using it, and keep using it? Any setup, learning or new habit it asks of them: up to four, each up to 9 words.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what they'll have to do, Keel shows the efforts back for me to check before I pick one to test, which is the obvious next step in the solution section.
screens.why2: Both rows are plain to me and to my wearers: 'caption glasses' is our own term, 'charge every day' is ordinary, and the intro tells me what to do in one line (though it repeats the title).
screens.why3: Both are steps my wearers take themselves in a normal week, putting the glasses on for a conversation and keeping them charged, so they can answer from their own life.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, each one step in the wearer's voice, with no overlap with Compatibility's phone and caption-reading rows or with buying the glasses.
screens.why5: The first row is my effort as revised, wearing the caption glasses in conversations, and the charging row is a true daily habit of my product that fits what I said.
screens.why7: Both rows meet the measure (their own effort, base-form verb, under 9 words, no other role's step), but the second reads as Keel's suggested habit without the why the card says a suggestion carries, and 'every day' is a number I never gave.
screens.instead: Keep 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' as my row; show 'Charge the glasses each night' as Keel's suggestion with its why (a new daily habit first use asks), set apart from my rows.

screens.why1: After I listed what wearers must do to start, picking the one most likely to stop them is the obvious next step before the stranger's test.
screens.why2: Wearing the caption glasses in conversations and charging them every day are exactly how I and my users talk about it.
screens.why3: I know from power users and returns which habits stick, so I can judge which effort is the real barrier.
screens.why4: Both rows are real efforts the wearer takes, but 'Wear the caption glasses in conversations' is the whole use rather than one effort, so it overlaps with everything after it; the one-time pairing to the phone is missing.
screens.why5: The pick is my own row as saved in revision 24, unreworded, and the belief says it back.
screens.why7: Both are the wearer's own steps on the one measure and the belief can be held or refuted, but the picked row reads as 'use it at all' rather than a distinct adoption effort, bending the card's rule that the row names an effort beyond using it.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? Wear the glasses out in conversations with hearing people · Charge the glasses every day · Pair the glasses to their phone once

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious moment to decide whether to collect emails from people who want to try the glasses, and I'd want early wearers for a $599 product with 15-day returns.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with the hint showing the exact line respondents will see is plain to me as a founder; I know what a pilot list is.
screens.why3: Whether I want a waitlist of deaf and hard-of-hearing people to follow up with is my own call, fully answerable.
screens.why4: Yes or no is complete and distinct for this toggle, in plain words, and no escape is needed for a founder's own setting.
screens.why5: It keeps my intent, but "try this for real" is vague for a physical product people would buy, not trial, and it would read better if it named the caption glasses or the free-returns order I typed as my commitment step.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? Hint: people who say yes see "Would you like to try the caption glasses yourself? Leave your email." -- Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who asks the questions belongs here, at the last step before the link goes out to strangers, after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: The question and the hint are plain to me, and the hint says up front that every question is also written on screen and can be answered by typing or tapping, which is the first thing I'd check for my people.
screens.why3: I can pick between two voices, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing adults what matters is whether the face is easy to lipread and the on-screen text is clear, and a 5-second audio sample tells me neither, so I'd be partly guessing.
screens.why4: The two choices are distinct, but each is offered as 'Hear Daphne · 5 s' with no way to see her face speaking or choose text-only, which is the option that fits an audience many of whom will not hear her at all.
screens.why5: It names my respondents as I typed them and leaks nothing of AirCaps to the people who will be asked.
screens.instead: Who should ask deaf or hard-of-hearing adults your questions? (every question is written on screen with captions; watch each speak to judge how easy her face is to lipread): Daphne ▶ Watch Daphne · 5 s / Saskia ▶ Watch Saskia · 5 s / Text only, no video

screens.why1: Choosing how the study reaches people belongs right after choosing who asks the questions and just before sending, so it is obvious why this is asked here.
screens.why2: Each option says plainly what the respondent would see and do, and I can pick on first reading.
screens.why3: I know my deaf and hard-of-hearing users read captions all day and many find a spoken video prompt harder than text, so I can answer this from my own work.
screens.why4: The three options are distinct and 'Let them choose' is a fair escape, but for this audience Daphne is described voice-first ('asks each question aloud', 'answer by talking'), and no option lets someone answer in ASL, which a signing Deaf respondent would need.
screens.why5: My pick 'Read and tap' is shown as typed, and nothing of the product or the roles leaks into the format choice.
screens.instead: How should deaf and hard-of-hearing adults answer? Read and tap (type or speak into boxes) / Daphne on video, captioned on screen, answer by typing, talking or signing / Let them choose.

screens.why1: Deciding who gets the interview link is the natural last step once the study is built and the interview mode is chosen.
screens.why2: The first and third options read plainly, but 'People I found with Keel -- From a search on the Contacts page' assumes I know a Keel page I have not seen in this flow.
screens.why3: I know whether I am sending to named people I know, a list, or posting in a deaf and hard-of-hearing community group, so this is answerable from my own work.
screens.why4: Named people, a found list, and one open link in a group cover the real ways I would reach deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, and they do not overlap.
screens.why5: It is a logistics screen that changes nothing I typed and shows nothing of AirCaps to a respondent.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (each gets their own link) / A list I build in Keel's Contacts (Keel makes a link for each) / A group where they already gather, like a DHH forum or Facebook group (one open link, each person signs in with Google)

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits under the title. The tally says 3 of 3 beliefs hold, and each card puts its own count (7 of 7) beside the bar of 5 of 7, so I can see why it held.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what was counted, over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: The three dimension names are mine and the beliefs are recognisable. But the statement under the title is garbled: "wearing the glasses the app on lightweight glasses shows..." and the captions clause is repeated. The Relative advantage line reads awkwardly against how I'd put it.
screens.why_b4: The page never says what three holding beliefs mean for AirCaps. It doesn't say whether to move on to price, or what to watch in the 3 conditional wearers.
screens.why_b5: n=7 is shown, but nothing says that 7 is a small sample for a unanimous result. "7 of 7 would do it" counts the 3 who set a condition as plain yeses, which is a soft overstatement.
screens.instead: Your solution is holding up with 7 people: all 7 could read captions while watching faces and said it would have helped a lot, but 3 of the 7 would only wear the glasses on a condition. Read those conditions before you price, and treat 7 as a first read, not proof.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it: 7 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the bar sits at 5 of 7 on the strip, all plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, and the condition I picked on the way in: could read captions while watching faces.
screens.why_b4: It tells me concretely that reading captions while watching faces won't block adoption and points me to adoption friction as the thing to look at.
screens.why_b5: The count line says this is 'a lean, not a call', but the So line still states flatly that this 'is not what will stop them' and that adoption friction is, which is firmer than 7 people answering a hypothetical can carry.
screens.instead: Say: 'All 7 who answered could, so far this doesn't look like the blocker, but it's a small group answering with the glasses only imagined; check adoption friction below.'

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decides it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who said better, over 7 people, with the marker at 5 on the strip; the doubled '7 7 a lot' is cramped but still readable.
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Relative advantage, and the belief uses my benefit, 'more of the talk followed without asking for repeats', against my hard case of losing the conversation with hearing people.
screens.why_b4: The So line says the imagined gain is unanimous and points me to Adoption friction, whether they would actually wear the caption glasses, as the real open question.
screens.why_b5: The screen flags the small n as 'a lean, not a call' and says the answers were hypothetical, but the question it shows described AirCaps as 'an app' rather than caption glasses, so 7 of 7 'a lot' may rest on a product they didn't picture.
screens.instead: Show the question as asked about AirCaps, caption glasses paired to your phone, so I can trust that the 7 'a lot better' answers are about the thing I sell.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside its deciding number, 7 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, with the 3 conditional yeses split out under it.
screens.why_b2: Yes 4 and the comfort condition 3 count for me, the two against rows are at 0, it is over 7 people, and the marker sits at 5. All of it is plain on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Adoption friction' and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are the step and belief I saved, and the stranger's question uses my own clause.
screens.why_b4: The So line promises that what would make it worth it to the 3 is below, but only Harriet's matinee trial speaks to that. Ruth's note asks for audience-question pickup and Tomás's describes his end-seat workaround, so I am not told concretely that comfort over a whole conversation is the catch to prove, for example through the 15-day returns.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the conditional yeses are split from the plain ones, and 'a small group: a lean, not a call' keeps a 7-of-7 from reading as a strong result.
screens.instead: 4 of 7 would wear them as is; 3 would only if they stay comfortable through a whole conversation. Lean on the 15-day returns (one says she'd want to try a pair at a matinee first) to prove comfort before they buy.

screens.why_b1: The box says Holding up with 7 of 7 would do it against a bar of 5 of 7, so the verdict and the number that decides it sit together.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would wear the caption glasses in conversations' are exactly the dimension and belief I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Adoption friction held, 7 of 7; what they added' is a generic lead-in. Nothing says what to do, like offering a try-on before ordering or testing lens readability in stage lighting and pickup of audience questions in big halls.
screens.why_b5: One label, 'Only if it stays comfortable through a conversation for' (ending on a dangling 'for'), is stamped on all three quotes, yet none of them is about comfort. Tomás's quote is even a workaround that suggests he may not need the glasses, so the 7-of-7 'held' reads stronger than these three conditions carry.
screens.why_b6: The quotes teach me things I did not type: a borrow-for-one-matinee try-first ask, lens readability under stage lights, audience-question pickup in big halls, and a one-sided-deafness seat workaround. But the single wrong theme label buries them instead of naming them.
screens.instead: Held 7 of 7 (bar 5), but 3 of 7 attach conditions: Harriet wants to try one matinee before ordering (a loaner or try-on beats free returns for her), Ruth needs audience questions picked up in a big hall, and Tomás already copes by sitting with everyone on his good side, so single-sided users may not need it.

screens.why1: As the opening screener it's obvious why it's asked: the study is about talking with hearing people, and I do that most days at work and at the shops.
screens.why2: "Hearing people" is how we say it ourselves, so I'd answer straight away.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I talk with hearing people in a week, because I do it all the time.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it for a gate, and no escape is needed here.
screens.why5: It's in plain words with nothing about a product or a company's plan showing through.
screens.why6: It's short and one question with two options, easy to catch once, provided I can see the captions or the screen.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, asking whether I got lost in one of those conversations this week is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: I'd say I 'lost track of' or 'got lost in' the conversation; 'lose the conversation' makes me read it twice, though I get what it means.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether I lost track at the shop counter, at work or at dinner this week; that is my own week.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, and both are true of someone: some weeks it's all one-on-one in quiet rooms and I follow fine, other weeks I'm lost at a noisy table.
screens.why5: It asks about the moment I couldn't follow, not the idea, with no product or company words; it drops the 'too fast or too noisy' detail, but losing track is the thing that hurts.
screens.why6: Short, one question, then 'Yes or no'; easy to take in once, and I'd likely see the captions too.
screens.why7: The gate asks about the problem (losing track), not the circumstance everyone has (talking with hearing people), so a No is truly possible and the share can hold or fail against the founder's band; there is no escape, as the card requires.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did you lose track of a conversation with hearing people? Yes · No

screens.why1: After two questions about losing the thread with hearing people this week, being shown an idea for that exact problem is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Captions, lens and eye contact are everyday words to me; I'd follow it on first reading, though 'an app on glasses' is a slightly odd way to put it.
screens.why3: It's about my own conversations: I know what it costs to look down at a phone caption and lose someone's face.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It reads as a plain description of captions in glasses with a stated belief about eye contact, and nothing in it talks about me in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It can be said, but it repeats 'people nearby' and 'inside the lens' twice each, and 'When the people nearby are talking, you wear...' makes it sound like I put the glasses on only when someone talks, so heard once it drags.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that captions nearby speech inside the lens. You wear the glasses while you talk, and you see live captions of what people are saying. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: Right after the glasses card, it makes sense to ask whether I could follow captions and still keep my eyes on people's faces, because that is the whole point of having them in the lens.
screens.why2: Captions and watching faces are my everyday words, since I lip-read and use live captions on my phone, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know from phone captions that looking down loses the faces, but I've never had captions in a lens, so in my last conversation I'd be partly guessing what I could have done.
screens.why4: Yes easily, most of the time, only sometimes and no cover it without overlap, and I can't tell fits if I really can't judge.
screens.why5: Nothing beyond the idea card reaches me; the question is in plain words about reading and watching, not the company's terms.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold, then the one escape; it says well.
screens.why7: It's an ability worded with the ability four in order plus I can't tell apart, and deaf people will genuinely split on reading text while lip-reading, so the belief can hold or fail.
screens.instead: Think of your last conversation with hearing people. Could you have read captions while watching their faces? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the captions question, asking whether these glasses would have helped the last time I lost the thread is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: "Would AirCaps have done that better" reads as if it would have lost the conversation better, so I had to read it twice to work out that it means helped me follow it.
screens.why3: I lose conversations every week, but my last one was at a shop counter, not around a table, so I would have to reach back to an older dinner or half guess.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover what I would say, in plain words, and "I can't tell" fits someone who has never worn caption glasses.
screens.why5: Calling it just "an app" drops the glasses and the captions in the lens, which is the part that matters to me because I could keep watching faces.
screens.why6: The four options and the escape say well as a short list, but the question runs about 30 words before the options, and "done that better" is hard to catch by ear.
screens.why7: The four fixed rungs and the escape apart are all there and the belief can be supported or refuted, but "done that better" leaves unclear which better is meant (the card's pitfall), and the table narrows the occasion.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time you lost the conversation with hearing people. Would AirCaps, glasses that caption speech in the lens, have helped you follow it, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about whether it would have done better, asking whether I'd actually put the glasses on is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Wear the caption glasses in conversations is plain to me on first read or hearing; I already know what captions are.
screens.why3: I know my own conversations, what I already wear and what I'd put up with, so I can answer this from my own life.
screens.why4: Yes, a conditional yes, probably not and no are distinct and cover my real answers, and staying comfortable through a whole conversation is a true catch for me with glasses on my face and aids behind my ears; I can't tell fits as the escape.
screens.why5: The glasses that caption speech come straight from the idea card I was shown, with no team jargon or the founder's terms for people like me.
screens.why6: Said aloud it is one short question and four short options I can hold, then the single escape, with nothing that only reads on the eye.
screens.why7: The effort is a habit I take on myself, the options run in the card's order with my own condition in the Only if, two count for and two against so the belief can hold or fail, and I can't tell is the one escape.

screens.why1: After three questions about the glasses, it makes sense to ask what would tip it for me before the study ends.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and it names AirCaps rather than a bare 'it', so I know what it's asking about on first hearing.
screens.why3: I know what would matter to me: captions that keep up when three people talk at once in a noisy restaurant, and glasses I wouldn't feel odd wearing at the theatre or dinner table.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: It uses only the name already given on the idea card, with nothing new about the product or the founder's terms reaching me.
screens.why6: One short question with no list, symbol or parenthesis, easy to hear once and answer.
